narrative:
The model predicted a 66.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly 6 among accepted students) signaled that you struggled significantly relative to your peers at that stage. Your first-year ranking had a smaller but still notable effect in the same direction, as you also placed in the bottom decile against an average around 6 for admitted students.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure. At 3.00 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, so the model saw some promise there. However, this positive signal was not large enough to offset the impact of your later class rankings.

Your low family income, LSAT score of 26.5 (well below the 37.18 average of accepted students), and full-time work plans also contributed to the overall picture, though they carried less weight than your law-school performance.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider targeted bar-prep programs that address specific weaknesses, and retake the LSAT if possible. These steps can demonstrate growth and raise your profile for future applications. (248 words)
